lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A simulation computes where bodies moved and how a surface changed. But numbers don't make a good talk. How do you turn them into a film?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I'm guessing that's where MistubaVideo comes in.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. It's a repository under the ETSim project that renders simulation exports with Mitsuba 3, a path tracer. There's a batch command for sequences of OBJ meshes, and a helper called mitsuba-video for richer recordings.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Recorded body poses and surface fields, through what it calls source adapters. One adapter reads a versioned manifest listing bodies, meshes, materials, poses and field images. Another reads a recording from a tool called TextureFriction.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And if I use a different simulator?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A small writer class lets another simulator export that same manifest format. So the renderer isn't tied to a single source.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What happens once the data is in?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It applies the recorded poses, then blends a base material and an affected material according to the surface field, so you actually see wear appear. Mitsuba 3 traces the light, and you can add a heatmap, a flattened UV atlas panel and a chart of the covered area.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Why render after the fact, rather than during the simulation?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Because you can change the camera or the lighting without repeating the simulation. That's the whole appeal.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A few commands. Inspect checks the input, preview checks camera and framing, render makes the frames with quality presets called preview, draft and paper. Then FFmpeg encodes the frames into an MP4.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So frames, heatmaps and video for reports and talks.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's it. The written page has the pipeline diagram.
